title: Titus
subtitle: Sound teaching for a young church on an island of liars
lead: Titus is a short letter from Paul to a coworker he left behind on Crete, a large island of many towns in the middle of the Mediterranean. The churches there were new and scattered, and some teachers were upsetting whole households with "Jewish myths", purity rules and arguments, for money. Paul tells Titus to appoint trustworthy elders in every town, to correct the troublemakers, and to teach every group in the church, old and young, men and women, slaves, how to live so that outsiders would see the gospel's goodness.

Between the instructions stand two of the richest summaries of the faith in the New Testament. In the first, God's grace "has appeared, with salvation for all people" and trains believers while they wait for "the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" (2:11-14). In the second, God saved us "in keeping with his mercy" through "the bath of new birth and the renewing by the Holy Spirit" (3:4-7). The letter is traditionally Paul's; most critical scholars think a follower wrote it, with 1 and 2 Timothy, in his name. This Plain follows the text and presents the questions fairly.
facts: Traditionally Paul (1:1). Most critical scholars hold that a follower of Paul wrote it in his name, together with 1 and 2 Timothy; many others defend Paul, perhaps with a secretary. See the topic The Pastoral Letters.
If Paul wrote it, after the end of Acts, in the 60s AD, between a first and a second imprisonment. If a follower wrote it, late first or early second century.
Not stated. Paul is free and plans to winter at Nicopolis (3:12), most likely the city in Epirus, western Greece.
Titus, Paul's Greek coworker, and through him the house churches of Crete (the closing grace is to "all of you", 3:15).
A letter of instruction to a delegate, with a long greeting, lists of qualities and duties, two creed-like summaries (2:11-14; 3:4-7), a "trustworthy saying" (3:8) and travel notes.
Greek, with many words found nowhere else in Paul's letters and much vocabulary from Greek ethics.
authorship: It opens "From Paul, a slave of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ" (1:1), names Titus as "my true-born child" (1:4), and ends with plans and names (3:12-15). Nothing in it says anyone else wrote it.

By the late second century the church quoted it as Paul's: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.4) cites 3:10 with "as Paul also says". Eusebius (Church History 3.4.6) later records that Titus oversaw the churches of Crete. On this view Paul visited Crete with Titus after his release from the imprisonment of Acts 28, left him there, and wrote from somewhere on the way to Nicopolis. The different style is explained by a different situation, a letter to a trusted delegate, or by a secretary.

Most critical scholars hold that the three Pastoral Letters were written together by a follower after Paul's death. For Titus in particular they point to the mission on Crete, which does not fit Acts (Paul only sails past Crete as a prisoner, Acts 27:7-21); church order with elders in every town; "faith" and "sound teaching" as a body of doctrine; and the new vocabulary. The full arguments for and against are set out once, on the topic page The Pastoral Letters.
Some hold that real notes of Paul, such as the travel plans of 3:12-14, were worked into a later letter. Others think a coworker such as Luke wrote for Paul. Neither view can be proved.

audience.to: Titus, a Greek believer who had worked with Paul for years (Galatians 2:1-3; 2 Corinthians 7-8), now left to lead the churches of Crete. Behind him stand the believers themselves: small house churches in several towns of a large island, made up of Gentiles and Jews (the opponents are "especially those from the circumcision", 1:10, and Philo names Crete among the islands with Jewish communities, Embassy to Gaius 282), of older and younger men and women, and of slaves, many in households headed by unbelievers. They had no settled leaders yet (1:5). They lived under Roman rule (3:1) among neighbors who judged them by the order of their homes (2:5, 8, 10) and who held a poor view of Cretans in general (1:12).
audience.why: Teachers were going from house to house teaching "Jewish myths", human commands, purity rules and genealogies, and charging for it (1:10-16; 3:9). The letter answers in three ways: leaders who hold to sound teaching (1:5-9); households whose good conduct silences criticism (2:1-10); and a clear statement of what God's grace has done, which is the ground of that conduct (2:11-14; 3:4-7). Knowing the audience changes the reading: the rules for wives and slaves are written to vulnerable people in a society that watched them, with the outward reason stated each time; the harsh line about Cretans is a quotation turned against troublemakers, inside a letter meant to make Cretans "sound in the faith".
views: Titus is a real letter to a real coworker on Crete, written by Paul between imprisonments, and also meant to be read to the churches to back Titus' authority.
A follower of Paul used Titus and Crete as a setting to give later churches a model of leadership and household order in Paul's name; the first readers were the churches of the writer's own time.

outline: Greeting: Paul, the hope of eternal life, Titus
Elders in every town: the overseer as God's steward
The teachers who must be silenced; the Cretan prophet; clean and unclean
Duties for older men, older women, young women, young men and slaves
The grace that has appeared and the appearing still to come
Once lost, now saved by mercy: the trustworthy saying
Foolish debates and the person who causes splits
Artemas, Tychicus, Nicopolis, Zenas and Apollos; greetings

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Titus against Crete under Rome: an island of many towns with Jewish communities, house churches in households of free people and slaves, the Greek reputation of Cretans, the travels of Paul's coworkers, and Nicopolis in Epirus. Asks what the first readers would have heard in each instruction.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the letter and when, how it relates to 1 and 2 Timothy, why the journey to Crete is missing from Acts, what the vocabulary and church order show, and how the text came down to us. Points to the topic page The Pastoral Letters for the shared arguments.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's shape: the long greeting, the lists of qualities and duties, the two "epiphany" passages (2:11-14; 3:4-7) that ground the instructions, the trustworthy saying, and the repeated words: sound, sensible, Savior, good works.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the disputes with "those from the circumcision", the "Jewish myths" and the purity rules as arguments among believers about Jewish practice, and the use of Israel's Scriptures in 2:14 and 3:6 (Exodus 19:5; Ezekiel 37:23; Psalm 130:8; Joel 2:28). Asks how these verses have been used about Jews and how Jewish readers hear them.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Titus as the churches have: Chrysostom's homilies, Calvin's commentary, the debates on bishops and elders, "the husband of one wife", the deity of Christ at 2:13, baptism and new birth at 3:5, and the duties of wives and slaves. Sets the churches' answers side by side.

sections.b:
Titus is a working letter. It is short, practical and full of lists, so it is easy to read it as a set of rules. But the lists are always tied to a reason. The elders' qualities answer the false teachers' faults. The household duties are grounded in the grace that "has appeared" (2:11). Gentleness toward outsiders is grounded in the memory that "we too were once" lost (3:3). Read the two summaries first (2:11-14 and 3:4-7), then the instructions in their light.

Key words are rendered the same way each time so a reader can follow them: "sound" (healthy) teaching; "sensible" for the Greek sōphrōn family; "godliness"; "Savior", used of God and of Jesus; "good works", the phrase that ends each section; and "This saying is trustworthy", the formula shared with 1 and 2 Timothy.

Titus is never named in Acts. Everything we know of him comes from Paul's letters. He was a Greek, taken to Jerusalem uncircumcised as a test case (Galatians 2:1-3). He carried Paul's difficult words to Corinth and came back with good news (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:6-15), organized the collection there (2 Corinthians 8:6, 16-23), and is called Paul's "partner" and "fellow worker" (2 Corinthians 8:23). This letter places him on Crete; 2 Timothy 4:10 sends him to Dalmatia. Later tradition made him the first bishop of Crete. See the topic Titus.

Crete is a long, mountainous island south of the Aegean Sea. In Acts its people appear at Pentecost ("Some are Cretans and Arabs", Acts 2:11), and Paul's prison ship sheltered along its south coast at Fair Havens before a storm drove it away (Acts 27:7-21). The Cretans had a reputation in Greek literature as liars, which the letter quotes (1:12). The island had Jewish communities, as Philo reports, which fits the opponents "from the circumcision" (1:10). See the topic Crete.

Titus and 1 Timothy are twins in purpose: both tell a delegate how to set a church in order and how to answer false teachers. Titus is shorter and simpler. It has no separate deacons and no enrolled widows; elders and overseer appear as one office (1:5-7); its list for leaders leaves out "not a recent convert", which suits a new church. It has fuller statements of the gospel than 1 Timothy (2:11-14; 3:4-7). The two lists of qualities are compared on the page for chapter 1.

sections.h: Titus in the life of the church
sections.b: Few books so short have been used so much. 1:5-9 stands in every debate about bishops and elders. 1:12 made the "Cretan liar" a byword. 2:13 was used in the debates over the deity of Christ. 3:5 is a key text in the teaching on baptism and new birth. 3:10, with its word hairetikos, gave English "heretic". The cards on the chapter pages set out where the churches differ.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the letter answers Crete's bad name point by point
spec.body: The letter seems to answer, one by one, the faults in the Cretan proverb it quotes (1:12). "Liars": God "does not lie" (1:2), and the elder keeps a grip on "the word that can be trusted" (1:9). "Wicked beasts": the elder is "not hot-tempered, ... not a man who hits people" (1:7), and believers are to be "forbearing" and gentle (3:2). "Lazy bellies": the elder is not a heavy drinker (1:7), older women not enslaved to wine (2:3), and the whole church must give itself to good works, "so that they will not be without fruit" (3:14). If this is deliberate, the letter turns the island's insult into a program: the gospel makes Cretans the opposite of their reputation. The link between 1:2 and 1:12 is plain in the text; the claim that the whole letter is built to answer the three charges is my own, and the evidence is circumstantial.

prompts: A young Greek man in a simple travel cloak standing on a rocky Cretan hillside above a small white town, holding a rolled letter, with a fishing boat on the blue sea below and the high mountains of Crete behind. Small groups of people, men and women, a slave carrying water, gather at the doors of houses. Sketched by hand on old parchment in ochre and charcoal, with cave-painting figures and soft modern watercolor washes; torn, uneven edges; no hard frame.

A seated poet on a stone bench with a lyre, his mouth open in speech, while a ribbon of Greek letters curls out and loops back on itself like a knot. Beside him a carved tomb with an empty dark doorway. Drawn like an ancient manuscript illumination mixed with modern ink sketching; earth colors; soft, irregular edges.

A dark scroll-shaped sky over a sleeping Mediterranean island town; a warm light breaks through the clouds and falls on households: an old man, an old woman teaching a young wife, young men, a slave at work, all lifting their faces. Charcoal and gold wash on parchment, in the style of a cave drawing crossed with a modern sketch; edges fading into the scroll.

A simple stone basin of water in a house courtyard; a person rising from the water with arms open; above, a dove-like shape pouring light like water from a jar. Hand-drawn on parchment with ochre, blue and charcoal; soft brush strokes; no square borders.
reading: Six sermons on the letter, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, vol. 13.
John Calvin, Commentary on the Epistle to Titus
Calvin's verse-by-verse commentary, important for the Reformed reading of elders and bishops (1:5-7) and of baptism (3:5).
Jerome D. Quinn, The Letter to Titus (Anchor Bible, 1990)
A full commentary on Titus alone, with an introduction to all three Pastoral Letters.
I. Howard Marshall (with Philip H. Towner), A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Pastoral Epistles (International Critical Commentary, 1999)
A detailed commentary on the Greek text that weighs every view of authorship.
Philip H. Towner, The Letters to Timothy and Titus (New International Commentary on the New Testament, 2006)
A large commentary that argues for Paul as author and reads each letter on its own terms.
Daniel B. Wallace, Granville Sharp's Canon and Its Kin (2009)
A study of the Greek construction behind 2:13, concluding that the verse calls Jesus God.
